589.title: Against harm
589.hook: a prayer against those who seek to harm; teachers stress praying against evil, not people
589.howItsDone: The twelfth blessing of the weekday Amidah, against slanderers and wickedness, appears in different wordings in different prayer books; many teachers explain it through Beruriah's reading that the prayer is for sins to end, not sinners.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer for fair judges. Your line was kindness and justice, from the same throne. Today, the hardest blessing in the Amidah to say well.
screen: `KINDNESS AND JUSTICE, FROM THE SAME THRONE.`

segments.voice: A group of thugs lives in Rabbi Meir's neighborhood. The Talmud doesn't say exactly what they did, only that they caused him a great deal of trouble. And Rabbi Meir, one of the great teachers of the Mishnah, does what plenty of us would do. He prays that they die. His wife, Beruriah, hears him. She's a scholar in her own right, one of the few women the Talmud quotes on points of law. And she asks him a question about a verse.
screen: `THUGS IN THE NEIGHBORHOOD.` → `RABBI MEIR PRAYS THEY DIE.` → `BERURIAH ASKS ABOUT A VERSE.`

segments.voice: The twelfth blessing of the weekday Amidah is a prayer against those who do harm. The Talmud, in Berakhot 28b, says it was added later than the others: Rabban Gamliel asked who could compose it, and Shmuel the Small stood up and did. That's how the eighteen blessings became nineteen. Its wording has changed many times over the centuries, and scholars still debate exactly whom it first meant. Today it asks that slanderers have no hope and that wickedness vanish, and it ends: blessed are You, who breaks enemies and humbles the arrogant. It's a prayer born of real danger. So how should it be said? Back to Beruriah, in Berakhot 10a. She points to Psalm 104. In the old Jewish translation: "Let sinners cease out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more." But the Hebrew letters for sinners, she says, can also be read as sins. Let sins cease. Then look at the second half: if the sins are gone, the wicked will be no more, because they'll no longer be wicked. Pray that they turn around. Rabbi Meir does, and the Talmud says they did. That story has shaped how many teachers read this blessing ever since. Even with real enemies, the target is the harm, not the person who might still change.
screen: `THE BLESSING ADDED LATER.` · `EIGHTEEN BECOME NINETEEN.` · `SINNERS, OR SINS?` · `PRAY THAT THEY TURN AROUND.` · then, large: `END THE HARM.`

segments.voice: Name one harm in your world, a bully at school, a cruel post going around, someone who keeps hurting someone you love, a wrong in the news, and let yourself feel the anger honestly. Then try Beruriah's move: separate the harm from the person, and hold the wish that the harm stop and, if you can manage it, that the person doing it turn around. If you pray, you can ask for that.
Against harm. The Amidah's twelfth blessing, the one added at Yavneh, read through Beruriah: let sins cease, not sinners.
Your line: end the harm. The wish is not for people to vanish, but for the harm to end. See you tomorrow.

590.title: For the ones who chose
590.hook: a blessing for the righteous, the pious and sincere converts
590.howItsDone: Al hatzaddikim is the thirteenth blessing of the weekday Amidah, praying for the righteous, the pious, the elders, the scholars and righteous converts; converts to Judaism say the Amidah with the same words, God of our fathers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing against harm, and Beruriah's let sins cease. Your line was end the harm. Today, the blessing that comes right after it, for the good.

A man named Obadiah, who has become a Jew, writes a letter to Moses Maimonides, in Egypt. His question is about the Amidah. Every day it begins: our God and God of our fathers, God of Abraham. But Obadiah's fathers weren't Abraham's children. Should he change the words, and say God of your fathers? Or say nothing at that line at all? Is he saying something untrue three times a day? Maimonides' answer is still read today.
screen: `A LETTER TO MAIMONIDES.` → `GOD OF OUR FATHERS?` → `SOMETHING UNTRUE, THREE TIMES A DAY?`

segments.voice: Maimonides writes back: say it exactly as written. Abraham is your father too. He's the father of everyone who comes under the wings of the Divine Presence. By custom, converts are named son or daughter of Abraham and Sarah. And in the thirteenth blessing of the Amidah, the community names them in its prayer: on the righteous, on the pious, on the elders of Your people, on the remnant of their scholars, on the righteous converts, and on us, may Your compassion be stirred. Give good reward to all who truly trust in Your name, and place our portion with them. Blessed are You, support and trust of the righteous. Look at that list. The converts, gerei hatzedek, stand right next to the righteous and the scholars. And the last item: and on us. The ordinary person praying adds themselves at the end of the list, hoping to belong in that company. The Torah tells Israel to love the stranger, the ger, a word the rabbis also use for a convert. In the old Jewish translation: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." And Ruth, whom tradition remembers as a convert, says to Naomi: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Her great-grandson is King David. In this blessing, the people who chose stand in the community's daily prayer.

segments.voice: Remember someone who chose to join a people, a family or a community they weren't born into: a convert you know, an in-law who learned all the family recipes, a neighbor who became a citizen. Think of what it cost them, the learning, the questions, the moments of feeling outside, and hold them with respect for a few breaths. If you pray, you can include them in this blessing.

591.title: Jerusalem rebuilt
591.hook: blessings for Jerusalem and for the line of David
591.howItsDone: The weekday Amidah's fourteenth blessing prays for the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the fifteenth for the branch of David; on the afternoon of Tisha b'Av the paragraph Nachem, a prayer of comfort, is added to the Jerusalem blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing that names the righteous converts. Your line was right beside the righteous. Today, a city and a family line.

At the end of a Jewish wedding, just before the cheering, the groom stamps on a glass wrapped in cloth. It shatters, and everyone shouts mazel tov. Many explain the broken glass as a memory of Jerusalem's destroyed Temple, brought into the middle of the celebration. Even here, the city is remembered. Three times a day, in the middle of the Amidah, there's a prayer that does the opposite of breaking. It asks for the city to be built.
screen: `A GLASS UNDER THE GROOM'S FOOT.` → `JERUSALEM, EVEN AT A WEDDING.` → `A PRAYER THAT BUILDS.`

segments.voice: The fourteenth blessing says: to Jerusalem, Your city, return in mercy, and dwell in it as You promised. Rebuild it soon, in our days, as an everlasting building, and quickly set up the throne of David within it. Blessed are You, who builds Jerusalem. Notice the tense. Not who will build, or who built. Who builds: an ongoing act, a work site that never closes. The fifteenth blessing goes on to the family of David: may the branch of David Your servant sprout soon, for we hope for Your salvation all day long. Blessed are You, who makes the horn of salvation sprout. Branch, sprout: the Hebrew is tzemach, a prophets' image for a king from David's line, whom Jewish tradition calls mashiach, the anointed one, the messiah. Reform Judaism has generally spoken instead of a messianic age, a repaired world, rather than one person; Orthodox Judaism keeps the hope of a king from David's line. Some early prayer texts found in the Cairo Geniza show that in the land of Israel these two were once a single blessing. The Psalms put it simply, in the old Jewish translation: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem." On the afternoon of the fast of Tisha b'Av, the day of mourning for the Temples, a paragraph of comfort is added right here. But on ordinary days the blessing isn't a lament. It's construction language. Rebuild. Sprout. Every day, a little more.
screen: `RETURN TO JERUSALEM IN MERCY.` · `WHO BUILDS: AN ONGOING ACT.` · `TZEMACH: THE BRANCH OF DAVID.` · `PRAY FOR THE PEACE OF JERUSALEM.` · then, large: `REBUILD.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing in your life that's broken and could, slowly, be rebuilt: a relationship, a neighborhood, your health after a hard year, your trust in yourself. Don't plan the whole thing; picture one brick, the first small piece that could go back in place, and hold the hope that it can be built, in its time. If you pray, you can join that hope to the prayer for Jerusalem.
Jerusalem rebuilt. The Amidah's fourteenth and fifteenth blessings: the city built in mercy, and the branch of David's line.
Your line: rebuild. The ending says who builds, not who built. Day five hundred ninety-one.

592.title: Hear our prayer
592.hook: here any personal request may be added in your own words
592.howItsDone: Shome'a tefillah is the sixteenth blessing of the weekday Amidah; many Jews pause within it to add personal requests in their own words and language, and someone keeping a private fast adds the prayer Aneinu here.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the city that's always being built. Your line was rebuild. Today, the last of the requests, and the one with a blank space in it.

The Amidah's words are fixed. Jews in Tokyo and Toronto say nearly the same sentences, in the same order, three times a day. Which raises a fair question. What if what you actually need isn't on the list? A scholarship. The courage to leave a bad job. Your dog's surgery on Thursday. A sister who hasn't called back. The prayer has an answer for that, and it's built into the very last request.
screen: `AS FIXED AS A PRAYER GETS.` → `WHAT IF IT'S NOT ON THE LIST?` → `THE LAST REQUEST.`

segments.voice: The sixteenth blessing says: hear our voice, Lord our God. Have pity and compassion on us, and accept our prayer with mercy and favor. Don't turn us away empty-handed, for You hear the prayer of every mouth. Blessed are You, who hears prayer. In Hebrew, shome'a tefillah. The Psalms put it this way, in the old Jewish translation: "O Thou that hearest prayer, unto Thee doth all flesh come." All flesh. Every mouth. Not only the eloquent, not only those who know the Hebrew. The Talmud, in Avodah Zarah 8a, records the rule: a person may ask for their own needs in this blessing. Any need. The fixed requests before it cover what a whole people needs: wisdom, forgiveness, healing, a good year, justice. This one leaves a gap for what only you need. And it doesn't have to be in Hebrew. The Mishnah already allows the Amidah to be said in any language a person understands, and personal additions are often whispered in whatever language the heart speaks first: English, Yiddish, Spanish, Russian, Amharic. Someone fasting privately adds a short prayer here too. It's like a long printed form that ends with one open box: anything else? The tradition holds the words steady for everyone, and then, near the end, steps back and says: now, in your own words.
screen: `SHOME'A TEFILLAH: WHO HEARS PRAYER.` · `EVERY MOUTH, ALL FLESH.` · `ANY NEED MAY BE ADDED HERE.` · `IN ANY LANGUAGE.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN WORDS HERE.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what you actually need right now, not what you think you should need, and let it be specific, even a little embarrassing: the exam, the bill, the conversation you're dreading, the loneliness on Sunday nights. Put it into one plain sentence, in whatever language comes first. If you pray, say it as a request; if not, simply say it to yourself, under your breath.
Shome'a tefillah. Who hears prayer: the Amidah's sixteenth blessing, where any personal request may be added, in any words.

593.title: We thank you
593.hook: everyone bows at "we give thanks"; the rabbis say this blessing is said by all
593.carry: no one can say it for you
593.howItsDone: Jews bow at the beginning and end of Modim, the thanksgiving blessing of every Amidah; during the leader's repetition the congregation says Modim d'Rabbanan quietly, and on Hanukkah and Purim the paragraph Al hanissim is added.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shome'a tefillah, the blank space in the Amidah. Your line was your own words here. Today, the asking is over, and the thanks begins.

When the leader repeats the Amidah out loud, the congregation mostly listens. They answer amen at the end of each blessing, and let the leader speak for them. You can be represented. Then the leader reaches one blessing, bows, and the whole room does something different. Everyone starts murmuring their own words, at the same time, quietly, as if to say: no, this one, I'll do myself.
screen: `THE ROOM LISTENS AND ANSWERS AMEN.` → `ONE BLESSING, EVERYONE BOWS.` → `THIS ONE, I'LL DO MYSELF.`

segments.voice: After a short blessing asking that prayer be accepted, called Retzeh, comes the eighteenth: Modim. It begins: we thank You, for You are the Lord our God and the God of our ancestors forever. Then it lists: for our lives, entrusted to Your hand. For our souls, in Your keeping. For Your miracles that are with us every day, and Your wonders and goodness at every time: evening, morning and noon. Not the parting of the sea. The miracles of every day. People bow at its first word and at its end, as they did at the start of the Amidah. And when the leader repeats it aloud, the congregation says its own quiet version, called Modim d'Rabbanan, the Modim of the rabbis. The Talmud, in Sotah 40a, collects the words several rabbis said here, and later commentators explain why everyone joins in: someone else can make a request for you, but no one can say thank you on your behalf. The word modim can mean both we thank and we acknowledge. In Genesis, when Leah has her fourth son, she says, in the old Jewish translation: "This time will I praise the LORD." And she names him Yehudah, Judah. The word Jew, tradition notes, goes back to Judah. So in a sense, the very name of the people is a thank-you. On Hanukkah and Purim, a paragraph about those miracles is added right here.

segments.voice: Count three ordinary things from today, one from the morning, one from the afternoon, one from now: a cup of coffee, a message from a friend, your lungs working without being asked. For each one, bow your head slightly, a small nod, the way you might to someone across a room. If you pray, you can say: we thank You.
Modim. We thank, we acknowledge. The Amidah's thanksgiving blessing, said with a bow, by everyone in their own words.

594.title: Grant peace
594.hook: the Amidah ends asking for peace, goodness and blessing
594.howItsDone: Sim Shalom is the final blessing of the Amidah, following the priestly blessing in the morning repetition; many Ashkenazi communities say the shorter Shalom Rav at the afternoon and evening services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Modim, the thanks no one can say for you. Your line was no one can say it for you. Today, the last blessing of the Amidah.
screen: `NO ONE CAN SAY IT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: So many things end on peace. Shalom is the word for hello and for goodbye. The Kaddish ends on it. So does the priestly blessing from the book of Numbers. Even the Mishnah, the great code of Jewish law, sixty-three tractates of rules about fields, festivals, courts and purity, closes its very last page with a sentence about peace. The Amidah follows the same pattern. After praise, after thirteen requests, after thanks, the very last thing it asks for is shalom.
screen: `HELLO, GOODBYE: SHALOM.` → `THE MISHNAH'S LAST PAGE.` → `THE AMIDAH'S LAST REQUEST.`

segments.voice: In the leader's morning repetition, just before this blessing, comes the priestly blessing. In the old Jewish translation, it ends: "The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." In Israel, descendants of the priests, kohanim, come forward and say it every day; in many communities outside Israel, they do so on festivals. Then the last blessing picks up the thread: Sim shalom. Grant peace, goodness and blessing, grace, kindness and compassion, to us and to all Your people Israel. Bless us, our Father, all of us as one, with the light of Your face. Blessed are You, who blesses Your people Israel with peace. The light of Your face is borrowed straight from the priestly blessing. All of us as one: peace is something no one can have alone. Shalom comes from a root meaning whole, complete. It's not only the absence of fighting. It's nothing missing. In many Ashkenazi communities, the afternoon and evening services use a shorter version, Shalom Rav, abundant peace. And that sentence on the Mishnah's last page? Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta says that God found no vessel that could hold blessing except peace, and quotes the Psalm: "the LORD will bless His people with peace." A vessel: all the other blessings, health, livelihood, wisdom, leak out without it. So the Amidah puts the container last, to hold everything that came before.
screen: `THE PRIESTLY BLESSING: GIVE THEE PEACE.` · `ALL OF US AS ONE.` · `SHALOM: WHOLE, NOTHING MISSING.` · `THE ONLY VESSEL THAT HOLDS BLESSING.` · then, large: `GRANT PEACE.`

segments.voice: Picture someone whose life feels un-whole right now, someone grieving, someone in a fight, someone pulled in too many directions. On each out-breath, send them one piece of what's missing: rest, calm, a quiet evening, a phone call that goes well. If you pray, you can ask for their shalom; if it's someone you're in conflict with, notice whether you can wish it for them too.
Sim Shalom. Grant peace. The Amidah's final blessing: peace, goodness and blessing, for all of us as one.
Your line: it's nothing missing. Peace holds all the rest. That's five hundred ninety-four days.

595.title: Guard my tongue (Berakhot 17a)
595.hook: the closing prayer: my God, guard my tongue from evil
595.carry: let my soul be like dust
595.howItsDone: After the final blessing of the Amidah, Jews say Elohai netzor quietly, then Psalm 19:15, then take three steps back, bow left, right and center while saying oseh shalom, and stand a moment before stepping forward again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sim Shalom, the vessel that holds every blessing. Your line was it's nothing missing. Today, the very last words before the three steps back.

A small experiment for the end of the day: count the things said about people who weren't in the room. The coworker's annoying habit. The friend's bad decision. The relative everyone sighs about. The tally can climb fast. Now look at where the Amidah puts its last request. The person praying has stood for several minutes, feet together, asking for wisdom, healing and peace. And as they get ready to step back into the day, the closing prayer worries first about one thing: the mouth.
screen: `COUNT WHAT GETS SAID ABOUT PEOPLE.` → `THE TALLY CLIMBS FAST.` → `THE LAST WORRY: THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: The Talmud, in Berakhot 16b and 17a, records the private prayers different rabbis said after they finished the Amidah. One of them, from Mar the son of Ravina, is the one printed in the prayer book today. It begins: Elohai, netzor leshoni mera. My God, guard my tongue from evil, and my lips from speaking deceit. It's built on a psalm. In the old Jewish translation: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile." Then: to those who curse me, let my soul be silent; let my soul be like dust to everyone. Open my heart to Your Torah. Notice the grammar has changed. The Amidah's requests speak as we: heal us, forgive us, bring us back. This prayer says my. My tongue. My soul. It began as one rabbi's personal prayer, and it still sounds like one. It ends with another psalm: "Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before Thee, O LORD, my Rock, and my Redeemer." Then the three steps back, a bow to the left, the right and the center, and oseh shalom: may the one who makes peace on high make peace for us. Remember drew near, and sefatai tiftach? The Amidah opened by asking God to open the mouth. It closes by asking God to guard it.
screen: `MAR SON OF RAVINA'S PRAYER.` · `MY GOD, GUARD MY TONGUE.` · `FROM WE TO MY.` · `OPEN MY LIPS, THEN GUARD THEM.` · then, large: `GUARD MY TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Pick the next hour of your day that will have people in it, a meeting, a family dinner, a group chat, and decide now: for that hour, nothing unkind about someone who isn't there, no eye-rolls, no small digs. Picture the moment the temptation will come, and the quiet you'll put in its place. If you pray, you can say the first line: my God, guard my tongue from evil.
Elohai Netzor. My God, guard. The personal prayer after the Amidah, asking to guard the tongue from evil.

Your line: let my soul be like dust. A week that prayed against harm, right beside the righteous, for Jerusalem, in your own words, with thanks, for peace, and now for a guarded tongue: the whole Amidah, walked. Day five hundred ninety-five.
